# Question 4 Draft Script (Praveen)

This R Markdown file contains work on question 4. The main analysis from this script should be adapted to fit into our group analysis script, and the main takeaways should be adapted to fit the final report.

### Question 4: Use any method to find either a simpler panel that achieves comparable classification accuracy, or an alternative panel that achieves improved classification accuracy. Benchmark your results against the in-class analysis.

We try both: a simpler panel using fewer of the in-class proteins, and an alternative panel using LASSO logistic regression.

## Load libraries and data

```{r, message = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(infer)
library(randomForest)
library(rsample)
library(modelr)
library(yardstick)
library(glmnet)

load("../../data/biomarker-clean.RData")
```


## Splitting Data Into Training and Testing

To compare everything fairly, we set aside a test set at the very beginning and only use it for evaluating accuracy at the end.

```{r}
set.seed(67)
biomarker_split <- biomarker_clean %>%
  initial_split(prop = 0.8, strata = group)

train_data <- training(biomarker_split)
test_data <- testing(biomarker_split)
```


## Baseline: In-Class Analysis

First we redo the in-class selection (top 10 proteins by t-test and by random forest, then a hard intersection) on the training data, so we have something to benchmark against.

```{r}
# function to compute tests
test_fn <- function(.df) {
  t_test(.df,
         formula = level ~ group,
         order = c("ASD", "TD"),
         alternative = "two-sided",
         var.equal = FALSE)
}

ttests_out <- train_data %>%
  # drop ADOS score
  select(-ados) %>%
  # arrange in long format
  pivot_longer(-group,
               names_to = "protein",
               values_to = "level") %>%
  # nest by protein
  nest(data = c(level, group)) %>%
  # compute t tests
  mutate(ttest = map(data, test_fn)) %>%
  unnest(ttest) %>%
  # sort by p-value
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  # multiple testing correction
  mutate(m = n(),
         hm = log(m) + 1 / (2 * m) - digamma(1),
         rank = row_number(),
         p.adj = m * hm * p_value / rank)

# top 10 proteins by t-test
proteins_s1 <- ttests_out %>%
  slice_min(p.adj, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)
```

```{r}
# store predictors and response separately
predictors <- train_data %>%
  select(-c(group, ados))

response <- train_data %>% pull(group) %>% factor()

# fit RF
set.seed(67)
rf_out <- randomForest(x = predictors,
                       y = response,
                       ntree = 1000,
                       importance = TRUE)

# top 10 proteins by RF importance
proteins_s2 <- rf_out$importance %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(protein = rownames(rf_out$importance)) %>%
  slice_max(MeanDecreaseGini, n = 10) %>%
  pull(protein)
```

```{r}
# hard intersection like in class
proteins_sstar <- intersect(proteins_s1, proteins_s2)
proteins_sstar
```


## Baseline: Logistic Regression and Evaluation

The `class_metrics` code from class gives an error. The newer version of yardstick only takes column names for `truth` and `estimate`, not things like `factor(class)`, so we make those columns with `mutate` first and then pass the column names.

```{r}
# metrics to report
class_metrics <- metric_set(sensitivity,
                            specificity,
                            accuracy,
                            roc_auc)

# make the factor columns first, then compute metrics
eval_fn <- function(.df) {
  .df %>%
    mutate(truth = factor(class, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE)),
           estimate = factor(pred > 0.5, levels = c(FALSE, TRUE))) %>%
    class_metrics(truth = truth,
                  estimate = estimate,
                  pred,
                  event_level = "second")
}
```

Since we're going to fit a lot of logistic regressions, we made a function that takes a set of proteins, fits on the training data, and evaluates on the test data.

```{r}
fit_panel <- function(proteins) {
  train_sub <- train_data %>%
    select(group, all_of(proteins)) %>%
    mutate(class = (group == "ASD")) %>%
    select(-group)

  test_sub <- test_data %>%
    select(group, all_of(proteins)) %>%
    mutate(class = (group == "ASD")) %>%
    select(-group)

  fit <- glm(class ~ ., data = train_sub, family = "binomial")

  test_sub %>%
    add_predictions(fit, type = "response") %>%
    eval_fn()
}

baseline_metrics <- fit_panel(proteins_sstar)
baseline_metrics
```


We save the baseline in one row so it's easy to compare against later.

```{r}
baseline_results <- baseline_metrics %>%
  select(.metric, .estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate) %>%
  mutate(method = "in-class (hard intersection)",
         n_proteins = length(proteins_sstar),
         proteins = paste(proteins_sstar, collapse = ", ")) %>%
  select(method, n_proteins, everything())

baseline_results
```


## Simpler Panel

To find a simpler panel, we order the baseline proteins by t-test p-value and fit a logistic regression for each panel size, adding one protein at a time until we reach the full panel.

```{r}
# order the baseline proteins by t-test p-value
proteins_ordered <- ttests_out %>%
  filter(protein %in% proteins_sstar) %>%
  arrange(p_value) %>%
  pull(protein)

# fit models using the top 1, 2, ..., k proteins
smaller_panels <- tibble(n_proteins = 1:length(proteins_ordered)) %>%
  mutate(metrics = map(n_proteins, ~ fit_panel(proteins_ordered[1:.x]))) %>%
  unnest(metrics) %>%
  select(n_proteins, .metric, .estimate) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = .metric, values_from = .estimate)

smaller_panels
```


We don't want to use the test set to pick the panel size, so we use 5-fold cross validation on the training data instead. For each panel size, we fit the model on 4 folds, compute the AUC on the fold left out, and average over the 5 folds.

```{r}
# 5-fold cross validation on the training data
set.seed(67)
train_folds <- vfold_cv(train_data, v = 5, strata = group)

# average cross validation AUC for the top k proteins
cv_auc <- function(k) {
  proteins <- proteins_ordered[1:k]

  fold_auc <- map_dbl(train_folds$splits, function(.split) {
    fold_train <- analysis(.split) %>%
      select(group, all_of(proteins)) %>%
      mutate(class = (group == "ASD")) %>%
      select(-group)

    fold_val <- assessment(.split) %>%
      select(group, all_of(proteins)) %>%
      mutate(class = (group == "ASD")) %>%
      select(-group)

    fit <- glm(class ~ ., data = fold_train, family = "binomial")

    fold_val %>%
      add_predictions(fit, type = "response") %>%
      eval_fn() %>%
      filter(.metric == "roc_auc") %>%
      pull(.estimate)
  })

  mean(fold_auc)
}

cv_results <- tibble(n_proteins = 1:length(proteins_ordered)) %>%
  mutate(cv_auc = map_dbl(n_proteins, cv_auc))

cv_results
```

We pick the smallest panel whose cross validation AUC is within 0.05 of the best one, and then check it on the test set.

```{r}
n_simple <- cv_results %>%
  filter(cv_auc >= max(cv_auc) - 0.05) %>%
  slice_min(n_proteins, n = 1) %>%
  pull(n_proteins)

proteins_simple <- proteins_ordered[1:n_simple]
proteins_simple

simple_results <- smaller_panels %>%
  filter(n_proteins == n_simple) %>%
  mutate(method = "simpler panel",
         proteins = paste(proteins_simple, collapse = ", ")) %>%
  select(method, n_proteins, everything())

simple_results
```

Cross validation picks a 3 protein panel (DERM, RELT, IgD). On the test set it gets an AUC of 0.766 and accuracy of 0.688, compared to 0.789 and 0.656 for the full 6 protein panel. So we can cut the panel in half and get about the same performance.
